strengths: Theoretically grounded framework: The paper derives the DMPO objective and mathematically formulates the data selection problem, proving that selecting samples with the most negative Preference Divergence (PD) term minimizes both the upper and lower bounds of the DMPO loss (Theorems 3.6 and 3.7).

Data-centric efficiency: The proposed selection approach aligns LLMs using only a 30% subset of the data. This not only yields superior performance compared to training on the full dataset, but also substantially reduces final DPO training time and computational costs.

Effective length bias mitigation: The paper addresses a critical challenge in reward/preference learning by integrating Length Balanced Sampling and Length Reward Penalty during proxy reward training. The ablation study (A2) clearly demonstrates how this prevents the propagation of length bias into the selected subset.

Comprehensive empirical validation: The method is rigorously evaluated on several diverse open-ended benchmarks (WizardLM, Self-Instruct, Vicuna, Koala, LIMA) and AlpacaEval 2, consistently outperforming full-data training, holistic preference baselines, and even the annotation-intensive Oracle baseline across multiple conflict levels.
weaknesses: Dependence on explicit sub-preference annotations: The proposed selection framework relies on the assumption that the input preference dataset has clear, fine-grained sub-preference labels to train the proxy reward models. It cannot be directly applied to standard preference datasets that only provide holistic labels.

Simulation-based evaluation: The conflict datasets are constructed synthetically from UltraFeedback by controlling sampling weights to simulate three explicit conflict levels. While this provides a controlled environment, evaluation on naturally aggregated, uncurated multi-source datasets would further strengthen the paper's real-world applicability claims.

Preprocessing overhead: Although final alignment training is highly efficient, the pipeline requires training proxy reward models on different sub-preferences (or a multi-task proxy model guided by system prompts). This adds an extra step and computational overhead prior to data selection, which should be explicitly discussed when comparing to single-step DPO selection methods.

Lack of comparison with multi-objective alignment baselines: While the related work mentions multi-objective direct preference optimization (e.g., MODPO), the experiments do not include empirical comparisons against these methods to show how data selection fares against direct multi-objective optimization algorithms.

strengths: The paper addresses a very practical and important problem: the limitations of standard holistic preference criteria in LLM alignment (e.g., ambiguity, inconsistency) and how to leverage more reliable fine-grained aspect-specific preference data.

Strong theoretical grounding: The authors derive the Direct Multi-Preference Optimization (DMPO) objective and mathematically prove (Theorems 3.6 and 3.7) that selecting samples with the most negative Preference Divergence (PD) values minimizes the upper and lower loss bounds of DMPO.

Comprehensive addressing of practical artifacts: The proposed methodology does not just stop at theory; it integrates crucial practical tricks, specifically addressing reward model comparability (quantile scaling) and length bias propagation (using length-balanced sampling and an explicit length reward penalty).

Solid empirical results: The proposed PD selection method achieves impressive performance, outperforming full-dataset training, holistic baselines, and even the annotation-expensive oracle across multiple benchmarks (AlpacaEval 2 and five open-ended datasets) using only 30% of the training budget.
weaknesses: The conflict scenarios are synthetically constructed/controlled from the UltraFeedback dataset. While this serves as a good testbed, evaluating on a real-world dataset that inherently exhibits natural, non-simulated conflicts among multiple aspects (without manual re-weighting or simulated assignment) would further strengthen the paper's claims.

The method introduces training pipeline complexity. Training $k$ proxy reward models (even with the 'all-in-one' system prompt approach mentioned in the appendix) and performing cross-reward evaluation on the entire dataset can be resource-intensive when the number of fine-grained aspects $k$ grows large.

The justification for the 'Oracle' baseline could be clearer. The paper defines Oracle as using the average of the four fine-grained scores. However, if these aspects are inherently in conflict, a simple average might not represent the optimal or desired human preference, making it questionable whether this baseline represents a true 'oracle'.

strengths: Strong Theoretical Grounding: The paper formally derives the Direct Multi-Preference Optimization (DMPO) objective and mathematically proves that selecting data with the most negative Preference Divergence (PD) values minimizes both the upper and lower bounds of the DMPO loss. This provides a rigorous foundation for the selection principle.

Computational and Data Efficiency: By utilizing a 30% selection budget, the proposed method reduces the final alignment training cost significantly. In Table 1, the total GPU hours for the proposed pipeline (18.6 hours, including proxy reward modeling and inference) is nearly half of the training time for the full dataset (33.6 hours) while achieving much better results.

Impressive Performance: The proposed method consistently and significantly outperforms all competitive baselines across varying levels of preference conflicts. It even beats the intensive Oracle baseline, which uses the average of all sub-preferences, demonstrating the benefit of consensus-based filtering.

Effective Mitigation of Length Bias: Incorporating length-balanced sampling and an explicit length reward penalty into the proxy reward models successfully prevents the selection of verbose, low-quality responses. This is clearly demonstrated in the ablation studies and the token length distribution visualizations (Figures B.7-B.9).

Clever Multi-Aspect Scaling: Using a single 'all-in-one' proxy reward model guided by system prompts to specialize in different sub-preferences is a highly efficient design choice that avoids training multiple distinct models.
weaknesses: Simulated Conflict Scenarios: Although the base dataset (UltraFeedback) is real, the different conflict levels (10%, 20%, 30%) are simulated by controlling the sub-preference sampling weights. Evaluating the method on an organically collected multi-preference dataset with natural conflict distributions would strengthen the real-world applicability.

Model Diversity: The evaluation is primarily focused on the Llama-3.1-8B model aligned via a Llama-3.2-3B proxy. Demonstrating the efficacy of this selection principle across other prominent model families (e.g., Qwen, Mistral) would confirm the universality of the proposed framework.

Reliance on LLM-as-a-Judge: The evaluation protocols heavily rely on Qwen2-Max and GPT-4o (AlpacaEval 2). While standard in the literature and partially mitigated by length-controlled metrics, incorporating some human evaluations or hard downstream task benchmarks would make the validation even more robust.
